newsitem.title: MOROCCO: Morocco looks into fee-paying education.
newsitem.headline: Morocco looks into fee-paying education.

text.p: A Moroccan education survey published on Tuesday showed 75 percent of people questioned opposed paying for their children's education.
The survey released during a news conference revealed that three-quarters of the 5,000 people who were asked across the country believed their children's studies should be free.
On Tuesday, Higher Education Minister Driss Khalil said this attitude had to be questioned.
"People have to learn to rely on themselves because the education budget weighs heavily on the state," he told the news conference held by the National Council of Youth and Future (CNJA).
Khalil said individuals should make some contribution to the costs of education to ease the burden on the state and enable it to improve the system.
Morocco devotes around 25 percent of its annual budget to all educational spending.

A CNJA spokesman said there was no question of charging for primary education. But the council was debating whether to suggest that couples earning more than 4,500 dirhams ($465) should pay something towards their children's secondary and higher education.
He said the money could be devoted to improving infrastructure the poor state of which was mainly responsible for illiteracy in rural areas which affect 78.7 percent of women.

"The main reason for the low numbers of people educated in rural areas is infrastructure, houses are scattered, no telephones, no roads and we have to gather people in one place to open a school," he added.
He added that education in Morocco overall did not fit into the needs of the employment market.

"Morocco has to take up the challenge of the free trade zone with Europe as it needs to upgrade its firms. It needs also to upgrade its educational system so that it adapts to the demands of employment.
